explanations.explanation: Close, but this one flips. Agur son of Jakeh says, “I have not learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One.” That sounds like a man with empty pockets. I think that's humility talking, friend, because he goes on to say a lot about God.

That's right, baker. Agur says, “I have not learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One.” He says it plain, no dressing it up. Then he turns around and talks about God's words being flawless. Humble start, strong finish.

explanations.answer: His name and His Son's name
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. After all those big questions, Agur asks, “What is His name, and what is the name of His Son…” He's asking about the One who gathered the wind and bound up the waters. Then he adds, “…surely you know!”

Good guess, but Agur doesn't ask where. He asks who has ascended to heaven and come down, but his question about this One is about names. He asks, “What is His name, and what is the name of His Son…” Nothing about an address.

That's a fine question, but it isn't the one Agur asks. He asks who established all the ends of the earth, not why. Then he asks, “What is His name, and what is the name of His Son…” The name is where he lands.
Yes, friend. Agur says, “Every word of God is flawless…” Every word, not just the ones I like. I've called my own batches flawless before, and the cookies had opinions.
Kings get a mention later in this chapter, but not here. Agur says, “Every word of God is flawless…” Advice from the palace is good for a lot of things, but the flawless one is God's word.
Elders are worth listening to, but that's not what Agur calls flawless. He says, “Every word of God is flawless…” That's the one he puts at the top.
That's right, baker. Agur says God “…is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.” A shield only works if you get behind it. Taking refuge means exactly that.

This one is true. Agur says God “…is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.” It comes right after he calls every word of God flawless. So he says God's word is flawless and God is a shield for those who run to Him.

Yes, friend. Agur says, “Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar.” If every word of God is flawless, there's nothing to fix. Notice the warning is about adding, not about learning.

Questions are fine, baker. Agur asks a whole row of them himself earlier in the chapter. The warning is “Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar.” Ask away, but don't tack anything on.

The text doesn't say anything about writing. Agur's warning is, “Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar.” It's about adding, not about copying. Copy away, just don't sneak in a new line.

explanations.answer: To keep lies far from him
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Agur asks, “Keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me.” That's his first request. Notice he asks God to keep lies away from him. That's a man who knows he needs help.

explanations.answer: To give him a long life
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Agur does say, “…do not refuse me before I die…” but his request is about something else. He asks, “Keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me.” Lies are what he wants held at a distance.
Agur never mentions enemies in his prayer. His first request is, “Keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me.” He's asking God to guard him from lies, not to win a fight.
It's the opposite, friend. Agur asks, “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion.” He turns down both ends. Riches aren't on his list.
Right. Agur says, “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion.” He doesn't ask for a pile of money or for empty shelves. He asks for his portion, and that's it.
Yes, baker. Agur says, “…I may have too much and deny You, saying, ‘Who is the LORD?’…” Having plenty could lead him to say that. So he asks for just his portion.
Losing riches isn't the reason Agur gives. He says, “…I may have too much and deny You, saying, ‘Who is the LORD?’…” His worry is what plenty could do to him, not what could happen to the plenty.
The text doesn't mention envy. Agur says, “…I may have too much and deny You, saying, ‘Who is the LORD?’…” His concern is about himself and God, not about what the neighbors think.

You got it, baker. Agur says, “Or I may become poor and steal, profaning the name of my God.” That's the other side of his worry. Too much and he might deny God, too little and he might steal. So he asks for the bread that is his portion.
Boasting isn't what Agur says. He says, “Or I may become poor and steal, profaning the name of my God.” Stealing is the danger he names for being poor.
Agur doesn't talk about wandering. He says, “Or I may become poor and steal, profaning the name of my God.” Poverty could lead him to steal, and he says that would profane God's name.

That's right, baker. Agur says, “Do not slander a servant to his master, or he will curse you, and you will bear the guilt.” Say something false about a servant and it comes back on you. The guilt lands on the one who slandered.
This one is true. Agur says, “Do not slander a servant to his master, or he will curse you, and you will bear the guilt.” It's a warning, and the guilt it names is yours. So the statement holds up.
Yes, friend. Agur says, “There is a generation of those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.” It's the first of his four generations. Fathers and mothers both show up in the line.
Close to home, but not the word. Agur says, “There is a generation of those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.” This generation's problem is how they treat their own parents.
Kings aren't in this line. Agur says, “There is a generation of those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.” Fathers are the ones being cursed here.

Careful, baker, it's the other way. Agur says, “There is a generation of those who are pure in their own eyes and yet unwashed of their filth.” They think they're clean, but they're not. I've felt spotless with flour all over my mustache.
Right. Agur says, “There is a generation of those who are pure in their own eyes and yet unwashed of their filth.” Pure in their own eyes isn't the same as clean. That's the gap he points out.

That's right, baker. Agur says, “…there is a generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men.” It's a hard picture. The ones being devoured are the oppressed and the needy.
Not this time. Agur says this generation is “…devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men.” The ones getting devoured are the oppressed and the needy. It's a heavy line.

Kings and princes aren't named here. Agur says they are “…devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men.” The ones on the receiving end are the oppressed and the needy. It's a heavy line.

Yes, friend, it's true. Agur says there are three things never satisfied, four that never say ‘Enough!’ Then he lists them: “Sheol, the barren womb, land never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, ‘Enough!’” He starts with three and lists four.

This one is true. Agur lists “Sheol, the barren womb, land never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, ‘Enough!’” Sheol is the realm of the dead. Four things, and none of them ever say enough.

explanations.answer: May the ravens of the valley pluck it out
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Agur says, “…may the ravens of the valley pluck it out and young vultures devour it.” I think this is one of the hardest lines in the chapter. He's talking about the eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother.

explanations.answer: May the lions of the field tear it apart
explanations.explanation: Agur doesn't name lions here. He says, “…may the ravens of the valley pluck it out and young vultures devour it.” Birds are what he names. It's a heavy line, and I think it hurts to read.

explanations.answer: May the jackals of the desert eat it up
explanations.explanation: Jackals aren't in this verse. Agur says, “…may the ravens of the valley pluck it out and young vultures devour it.” The birds he names are ravens and young vultures. It's a heavy picture, and I think it hurts to read.

Yes, friend. Agur says, “There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand…” Then he lists the eagle, the snake, the ship and the man with a maiden. For a man who started the chapter saying he's ignorant, he sure notices a lot of wonders.
Danger isn't the word he uses. Agur says, “There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand…” The word he gives is wonderful.

Distance isn't what he says. Agur says, “There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand…” Wonder is the word. Even an eagle in the sky and a ship at sea are things he stands in awe of.
That's right, baker. Agur says, “This is the way of an adulteress: She eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done nothing wrong.’” She says she has done nothing wrong. It's a serious picture.

explanations.answer: I am sorry for what I did
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Agur says. He says she “…eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done nothing wrong.’” No sorry in sight. What she says is that she has done nothing wrong.
Agur doesn't give her those words. He says she “…eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done nothing wrong.’” She doesn't ask for secrecy. She just says there's nothing to be sorry for.

explanations.answer: A maidservant who takes her mistress's place
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Agur's list ends with “…a maidservant who supplants her mistress.” That's the fourth thing the earth cannot bear up under. It comes right after an unloved woman who marries.

explanations.answer: A daughter who leaves her father's house
explanations.explanation: That isn't on Agur's list. The last item is “…a maidservant who supplants her mistress.” It comes right after an unloved woman who marries.

explanations.answer: A son who takes his father's land
explanations.explanation: Not on this list, baker. Agur's last item is “…a maidservant who supplants her mistress.” Land and inheritance don't come up in these four.

explanations.answer: Store up their food in summer
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Agur says, “The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer…” Small, but they plan ahead. Wise little things.

Agur doesn't say that about the ants. He says, “The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer…” The wise thing he names is storing up food in summer. A leader isn't mentioned.
It's the reverse. Agur says the ants “…store up their food in the summer…” They're working while the getting is good. I'd be the one napping.
Yes, friend. Agur says, “…the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation…” No king, and they still advance in formation. That's the kind of order I'd love in my kitchen.
This one is true, friend. Agur says, “…the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation…” No king, and they still advance in formation. FALSE? The locusts would like a word.

That's right, baker. Agur says, “…the lizard can be caught in one’s hands, yet it is found in the palaces of kings.” Small enough to catch, and still in the palace. Fourth on his list of small things that are wise.
The temple isn't what Agur says. He says the lizard “…is found in the palaces of kings.” Palaces, plural. That's quite an address for something you can catch in your hands.

City gates aren't in this verse. Agur says the lizard “…is found in the palaces of kings.” It can be caught in one’s hands, and that's still where it's found. Meanwhile I can't get through a phone menu without pressing zero five times.
Other way around, friend. Agur says the lion is “…mighty among beasts, refusing to retreat before anything…” No backing up. I retreat from a spider in the pantry, so I respect that.
Right. Agur describes “…a lion, mighty among beasts, refusing to retreat before anything…” It doesn't back down. That's why it makes his list of things stately in their stride.
Yes, baker. Agur finishes the list with “…a king with his army around him.” The lion, the rooster and the he-goat come first. All four are impressive in their walk.
No shepherd on this list. Agur's fourth is “…a king with his army around him.” A king with his army makes for a mighty walk.

Prophets aren't named here. Agur's fourth is “…a king with his army around him.” The first three are a lion, a strutting rooster and a he-goat, so the king and his army walk in that company. A rooster in that lineup gets me every time.

explanations.answer: Put your hand over your mouth
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Agur says, “If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth.” Stop talking. My mustache already covers my mouth, so I'm halfway there.
Agur doesn't send anyone to the elders. He says, “If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth.” His answer is to go quiet.
Agur doesn't mention bowing to a king here. He says, “If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth.” Hand over the mouth is the move.

You got it, baker. Agur says, “For as the churning of milk yields butter, and the twisting of the nose draws blood, so the stirring of anger brings forth strife.” Churn milk and you get butter. Stir anger and you get strife.
Sorrow is a fair guess, but it isn't Agur's word. He says, “…so the stirring of anger brings forth strife.” Butter from churning, blood from twisting, strife from stirring anger.
Shame isn't what Agur says. He says, “…so the stirring of anger brings forth strife.” Each action gives its result. Stirring anger gives strife.
